chunks: And by this same chain of transmission, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurara, who said:
I said to him: 'A man sleeps while he is in a state of wudu — does one nodding-off, or two, oblige him to perform wudu?'
He said: 'O Zurara, the eye may sleep while the heart and ear do not sleep. So when the eye, the ear, and the heart all sleep, then wudu has become obligatory.'
I said: 'What if something moved beside him and he did not know of it?'

He said: 'No — not until he is certain that he has slept, until a clear matter arises from that. Otherwise he remains upon certainty of his wudu, and certainty is never nullified by doubt — it is nullified only by another certainty.'

key_terms.الْخَفْقَةُ: a single nodding-off; brief involuntary lapse into unconsciousness
key_terms.الْيَقِينَ: certainty (yaqin); a legally established presumption that persists until positively overturned
key_terms.بِالشَّكِّ: by doubt (shakk); through mere uncertainty without contrary evidence
key_terms.وُضُوءٍ: wudu; the state of ritual purity required for prayer

ai.seo_question: Does nodding off during sleep break wudu, and what is the Shia hadith source for the principle that certainty is never nullified by doubt?
ai.summary: Zurara ibn A'yan asks the Imam whether light drowsiness (khafqa) during sleep nullifies wudu, and the Imam clarifies that ritual purification is only obligated when all three faculties — eye, ear, and heart — sleep simultaneously, not from a mere doze. The hadith culminates in the landmark Shia jurisprudential maxim that certainty (yaqin) of wudu is never overridden by mere doubt (shakk), establishing the foundational usul al-fiqh principle of istishab (presumption of continuity of an established state).
